3.add: Each discharge therefore samples a different image, because the fish and the object change position between pulses, and the model estimates the image from measured behavior and a biophysical description of the field.

4.add: The fish identified features associated with the positive object, and test trials with unfamiliar alternatives showed that the learned preference was not tied to a single comparison.

5.add: The sphere carried most of the preference, so recognition relied selectively on learned features of the object, and the cone and the narrow junction contributed less.

6.add: The fish nevertheless chose the smaller cube across distance combinations, which shows compensation for distance-dependent changes in the electric image.

8.add: Recognition depends on the usable object-induced perturbation relative to sensory noise and on the task, so the 4 cm range describes the tested discriminations. An electric field is physically present beyond this distance, and the grid held the minimum inspection distance fixed.

third_paragraph.9: The coordinated changes show that natural electrolocation input is sampled through changing movements and pulse intervals, so the sequence of electric samples depends on how the fish inspects the object.
third_paragraph.10: The reconstruction describes the information available to the fish: the current electric pattern and its recent history. Using that history to estimate object distance is a proposal that links electrosensory flow to the approach behavior.
third_paragraph.11: A single spatial measurement is less reliable under natural postures and body curvature, which motivates examining information distributed across successive samples. Static cues remain available within each sample.
third_paragraph.12: The relative gradient is a candidate cue in the reconstructed sensory input that reduces the dependence of the signal on object size. Using it requires an estimate of the movement of the fish, which links the approach behavior to the electric images.
third_paragraph.13: Simulations of cubes and spheres of 1, 2 and 3 cm with different electrical properties specify the conditions under which the proposed cue is robust. Distance information in the relative gradient survives changes in size, shape and conductivity that strongly alter the absolute signal.
third_paragraph.14: Overlapping gradients at different positions mean that receptors along the body can contribute to the same distance estimate in the tested reconstruction. A cue of this kind tolerates changes in posture and body curvature better than a local amplitude.
third_paragraph.15: The values describe cue analysis. The 6 cm criterion of the dynamic cue and the 3 cm criterion of the static measure are consistent with the roughly 4 cm recognition range of the choice tasks, because identifying shape and extracting a distance-related signal are distinct demands.

17.add: Learning speed depended on which senses were available and on whether the fish was emitting discharges. Training with both senses was fastest, and electrically silenced fish learned the visual task in about 6 days.

18.add: Two sensory streams about the same near object improved accuracy above that of vision alone.

third_paragraph.19: Electric dominance is conditional on the near-field task and the training history of the animal. The tests measure which sensory information controls the choice at a 1 cm inspection distance.

20.add: Visually trained and electrically silenced fish could learn the task, so the reliability of each stimulus stream determines how much it contributes.

21.add: The timing of the first spike therefore carries local amplitude, and the interval between sensing pulses influences that timing.

third_paragraph.22: Adaptation means that the same immediate amplitude can occur under different sensory histories and evoke different latencies. A central decoder interpreting latency must therefore take into account the mean level that precedes the amplitude change.

23.add: A latency shift is therefore interpreted together with how recently the receptor was stimulated, and individual afferents differ in the slope and position of their relationships.

third_paragraph.24: The replay experiment establishes history dependence at the sensory afferent. Latency followed the natural sequence of pulse intervals, so the afferent code carries the time structure of active sampling together with the electrical contrast being sampled.
third_paragraph.25: The first spike is therefore the principal timing variable for these responses. Later spikes can still influence synaptic transmission, even though their timing contributes little independent information about stimulus amplitude.
third_paragraph.26: Sensitivity to amplitude is a state-dependent transformation that changes with the sustained sampling rate and is not a fixed gain of the fiber. Coding models of the afferent therefore include the sampling rate as a variable.
third_paragraph.27: Published models fitted to afferent data support a description of history-dependent coding in which latency depends on both the current amplitude and the preceding intervals. Models that include interval-dependent sensitivity predict the measured latencies better than models that use amplitude alone.
third_paragraph.28: The slice preparation establishes local synaptic properties of ELL. Anatomical identification and pharmacology identify which pathways and receptors contribute to the recorded response, and brief stimulation of deep afferents and parallel fibers allows the two inputs to be compared.
third_paragraph.29: The pharmacological dissociation separates arriving spikes from the local postsynaptic response they evoke. Cadmium and tetrodotoxin identify the two components more securely than the latency or polarity of the waveform alone.

30.add: Their contribution links transmitter release to postsynaptic depolarization, and the reduced portions of the evoked response indicate that both receptor classes participate.

third_paragraph.31: Ligand-gated receptors provide the ionic conductances through which synaptic input changes membrane voltage. GABA-A and glycine receptors both contribute to deep-input inhibition in the slice, so the inhibition is not mediated by one transmitter system.

32.add: Parallel-fiber input to the medium ganglion cell therefore produces a brief window of excitation that inhibition through GABA-A receptors then limits.

33.add: Facilitation at intervals near 30 ms means that a second parallel-fiber volley evokes a larger response than the first.

third_paragraph.34: A single identified cell can express a large broad spike and smaller narrow spikes. The waveform differences constrain propagation and integration mechanisms, and in vivo experiments relate these spike types to circuit output and learning.
third_paragraph.35: The results connect pathway recruitment to membrane excitability. Deep stimulation and parallel-fiber stimulation produce different synaptic potentials, and the firing of the recorded neuron reflects the combined influence of those potentials and the spike threshold.
third_paragraph.37: Spatially distributed input can reach dendrites across an organized sensory structure, because the parallel fibers conduct the signal along their length. The distance-dependent latency is a physical transmission property of the pathway in the slice.
third_paragraph.38: The recordings support integration of self-generated context with sensory information. A corollary signal marks the timing of the discharge of the animal itself, and the neuron combines it with input from the electroreceptors.
third_paragraph.39: The circuit interpretation separates immediate output from an event that regulates subsequent synaptic change. N spikes deliver the output of the cell, and B spikes carry information that guides plasticity at the parallel-fiber synapses.

40.add: The recordings establish temporal relationships between the two spike types, and pharmacological manipulation and conductance measurements supplied additional evidence about the inhibitory mechanism.

41.add: The compartments participate in one circuit, and output and plasticity are influenced differently by incoming sensory and central signals.

42.add: B-spike activity after the stimulus ends reflects the preceding stimulation, with the command signal as the temporal reference.

43.add: The conductance analysis separates the excitatory and inhibitory contributions to the command-evoked response.

44.add: Disinhibition therefore releases the dendritic event at the ventral molecular layer, where the injection was made.

45.add: The results connect command context, dendritic events, synaptic strength and axonal activity, so the timing of a B spike determines whether the response to a command is reduced or enhanced.

inserts.title: Electric organ discharges are the active probe
paragraphs: A weakly electric fish generates brief electric organ discharges, or EODs, with a specialized organ and senses the current that returns through the water to receptors in its skin. The fish supplies the signal that it senses, so it does not depend on external fields.

Von der Emde and colleagues studied the elephantnose fish, _Gnathonemus petersii_, which emits a series of short pulses. Objects that conduct better or worse than the water change the current at the skin during each pulse.

Because each pulse is a discrete sample, the interval between discharges determines how often the fish updates its picture of the nearby scene. The fish can change this rate while it inspects an object.
notes: Active electrolocation uses a signal that the animal generates itself.
The probe.
The electric organ produces brief discharges, called EODs.
The fish senses the current that returns to its skin.
Why objects matter.
An object with conductivity different from the water changes the local electric field.
The change appears as a perturbation in current at the skin.
Species.
The elephantnose fish, Gnathonemus petersii, is a weakly electric fish that emits brief pulses.
Sampling in time.
Each discharge is a separate sample of the scene.
The interval between discharges sets how often the sample is updated.
Control by the animal.
The fish can change its discharge rate as it approaches an object.
Sensing therefore depends on both the object and the behavior of the fish.
Why a probe helps.
An animal that emits its own signal can sense in darkness and in murky water.
The fish controls when and how often it samples the surroundings.
Link to behavior.
Von der Emde and colleagues showed that recognition persisted in complete darkness, so the electric sense alone supported it.

inserts.title: Conductivity contrast perturbs the electric field
paragraphs: Conductivity is the ability of a material to carry electric current. An object that conducts better than water draws current toward it, and an object that conducts worse deflects current away. A smaller conductivity difference produces a weaker perturbation, so the size of the effect depends on how different the object is from the water.

Hofmann and colleagues used metal cubes, which conduct far better than water, and compared object-present and object-absent conditions. The difference between the two conditions isolates the perturbation caused by the object along the sensory surface.

The size and position of the perturbation depend on the object and on the position of the fish. The fish therefore reads the perturbation as a spatial pattern of increased or decreased current across its skin.
notes: The electric image arises from a difference in conductivity between an object and its surroundings.
Conductivity.
Conductivity describes how well a material carries current.
The tank water had a conductivity near 100 microsiemens per centimeter.
Direction of the effect.
A better conductor draws current toward itself.
A poorer conductor deflects current.
Experimental comparison.
Metal cubes were compared with the object-absent condition.
The difference isolates the perturbation caused by the object.
Dependence on position.
The pattern depends on both the object and the position of the fish.
What the fish receives.
The perturbation appears as a spatial pattern across the sensory skin.
Reading the field.
The perturbation is spread across many receptors in the skin.
Each receptor reports the current at its own position.
Metal cubes.
Metal is a much better conductor than water, so metal cubes produce a strong perturbation.
This makes them convenient objects for measuring the electric image.

inserts.title: Size constancy requires compensating for distance
paragraphs: Size constancy is the identification of physical object size despite changes in the sensory image. A distant object produces a weaker and broader electric image than a near one, so an observer that reads only the image would confuse a small near object with a large distant one.

Von der Emde and colleagues trained a fish to choose a smaller cube over a larger cube and then varied the distances independently. The fish kept choosing the smaller cube across distance combinations, with useful performance to about 4 cm.

Measured image diameter increased when a small cube moved farther away, so image width alone did not preserve physical size. The choices therefore show that the fish used distance information together with the image to identify the physical size of the cube.
notes: Size constancy asks whether an animal judges the object and not just the image.
The problem.
Distance changes the size and strength of the electric image.
Image alone does not specify the size of the object.
Training.
A fish was trained to choose a smaller cube over a larger cube.
The cubes were initially placed at 2 and 3 centimeters from the gates.
Test.
The distances of the two cubes were varied independently.
The fish kept choosing the smaller cube.
Image measurements.
Image diameter increased when a small cube moved farther away.
Controls.
Tests in darkness preserved the size discrimination, so the choices did not depend on vision.
Why distance matters.
A distant object produces a broader and weaker image than a near one.
The same image could come from a small near object or a large distant one.
Range of performance.
Useful performance extended to about 4 centimeters.
Beyond that the discrimination was no longer reliable.

inserts.title: A grid fixes the minimum inspection distance
paragraphs: A grid between the fish and the objects prevents the fish from approaching closer than a set distance before it chooses. The grid therefore fixes the distance at which each choice is made. The distances were measured from the grid to the metal objects, which stayed fixed during a trial.

Von der Emde and colleagues moved metal objects from 1 to 8 cm from the grid. Performance declined with increasing distance, and the tested shape and size discriminations failed beyond approximately 4 cm.

Fixing the distance prevents the fish from solving a trial by swimming directly beside the object. The measured range describes how far from an object the fish can still extract the features needed for the choice.
notes: Distance has to be controlled to measure a range.
The grid.
A grid prevented the fish from approaching closer before making a choice.
Distances tested.
Metal objects were moved from 1 to 8 centimeters from the grid.
Result.
Performance declined with distance.
The tested discriminations failed beyond approximately 4 centimeters.
Why the grid matters.
Without it, the fish could solve every trial by moving directly beside the object.
Meaning of the range.
The recognition range is the distance over which the animal identifies a tested object reliably.
Why a minimum distance.
If the fish could approach each object freely, the closest approach would determine the choice.
The grid prevents that shortcut.
Interpreting the limit.
The tested shape and size discriminations failed beyond about 4 centimeters.
An electric field extends farther than this, so the limit describes the usable information.
Summary of the range.
Within about 4 centimeters the fish identified shapes and sizes of metal objects, and it failed at greater distances in the same tasks.

inserts.title: A relative gradient divides change by amplitude
paragraphs: A gradient is the rate at which a quantity changes. A relative gradient divides the rate of change of the electric image amplitude during movement by the amplitude itself, so it expresses the change in proportion to the signal. The measure is calculated from the movement of the fish through the field.

Hofmann and colleagues compared absolute amplitude with the relative gradient for approaches to cubes of different sizes. Absolute amplitude depended strongly on size, whereas the relative-gradient curves overlapped much more closely across sizes.

Dividing by amplitude removes the factor that depends on the size of the object. The remaining value changes systematically with distance, which makes it a candidate cue for how far away an object is.
notes: Dividing a change by its own size can cancel something that is not wanted.
Definition.
A relative gradient expresses how rapidly the amplitude changes during movement relative to the current amplitude.
Comparison.
Approaches to metal cubes of different sizes were reconstructed.
Absolute amplitude and the relative gradient were compared.
Result.
Absolute amplitude depended strongly on object size.
Relative-gradient curves overlapped across sizes.
Why this helps.
The size of the object scales the amplitude, and division removes that scaling.
The remaining value keeps a systematic relation to distance.
Sampling.
Naturally adapted sampling supplied more measurements near the object than unadapted emission and movement patterns.
Candidate cue.
The relative gradient is an analysis of the reconstructed sensory input.
It is a candidate distance cue and is not a measured neural signal.
Near the object.
Near the objects, naturally adapted sampling supplied more measurements than a comparison pattern of unadapted emission and movement.

inserts.title: A learning criterion defines when a task is acquired
paragraphs: A learning criterion is a fixed level of performance that marks acquisition of a task. Schumacher and colleagues used more than 75% correct choices on three consecutive training days. Training days were counted from the start of the task until the criterion was met.

Mean training durations in intact fish were about 12.5 days with both senses, 16.2 days with electric input and 31.5 days with visual input. Electrically silenced fish learned the visual task in about 6 days.

A common criterion makes the durations comparable across conditions. The differences show how the available senses and the emission of discharges affected the speed of learning. A longer duration means that more training was required to reach the same level of accuracy, and a shorter duration means less.
notes: A criterion allows learning speeds to be compared between groups.
Definition.
Task acquisition is the development of the learned choice during training.
Criterion.
More than 75 percent correct choices on three consecutive training days marked acquisition.
Conditions.
Fish were trained with both senses, with electric information alone or with visual information alone.
Durations.
Both senses took about 12.5 days, electric input about 16.2 days and visual input about 31.5 days in intact fish.
Silenced fish.
Electrically silenced fish learned the visual task in about 6 days under the tested conditions.
What differs between conditions.
With both senses the fish could use electric and visual information together.
With one sense removed it relied on the remaining sense.
Interpretation.
The fastest learning occurred with both senses, and learning with vision alone was slowest in intact fish.
Why compare groups.
The same criterion applied to every group means that a longer training duration reflects slower learning.
Differences in duration are the measure of task acquisition.

inserts.title: Cue conflict tests which sense controls a choice
paragraphs: A cue conflict presents two senses with different information about the same object. The choice that the animal makes shows which sense controls the behavior when the two disagree. A conflict can be created by removing the useful information from one sense.

Schumacher and colleagues trained fish with electrically conspicuous metal objects and then tested choices with only electric or only visual information available. At an inspection distance of 1 cm, electric information strongly supported the trained discrimination. Tests were conducted with electric-only or visual-only information available.

Removing discriminating electric cues could impair use of visual shape. Electrosensory capture, the dominance of electric over visual information, therefore operates in the near field and depends on the training of the animal.
notes: Conflict between senses reveals their relative weight.
Cue conflict.
Two senses carry different information about one object.
The choice shows which sense controls the behavior.
Training.
Fish learned with electrically conspicuous metal objects.
Tests.
Choices were then tested with electric-only or visual-only information.
Result at 1 centimeter.
Electric information strongly supported the trained discrimination.
Removing the electric contrast could impair the use of visual shape.
Scope.
The dominance depends on the near-field task and on the training history of the animal.
Training history.
The fish learned the task with metal objects that gave strong electric contrast.
That experience made the electric stream a reliable source of information.
Scope.
The result depends on the 1 centimeter inspection distance and on the learned task.
Electric dominance.
Electrosensory capture is dominance of electric information over conflicting visual information.
It was strongest when the objects were close to the fish.
Measured quantity.
The tests measure which information controls the choice and not the strength of any particular synapse.

inserts.title: First-spike latency encodes stimulus amplitude
paragraphs: Latency is the time from a stimulus to the first spike of a neuron. A neuron can signal a stimulus by when it fires as well as by how often it fires. In mormyrids the mormyromast is the electroreceptor organ used for active electrolocation.

Sawtell and colleagues varied the amplitude of brief electric pulses that mimicked an EOD while recording mormyromast afferents. A larger amplitude shortened the first-spike latency, so the time of the first spike reported local amplitude.

A latency code is fast, because it needs only one spike per pulse. The brain can read amplitude from spike time within each discharge cycle, which suits an animal that samples the scene in discrete pulses.
notes: Spike timing carries amplitude in the electroreceptor afferents.
Definition.
Spike latency is the interval between the stimulus and the first action potential of the afferent.
Experiment.
Local electric pulses mimicked an EOD.
Their amplitude and timing were varied while afferent spikes were recorded.
Result.
An amplitude increase generally shortened first-spike latency.
Meaning.
Receptor input is represented partly by when a spike occurs and not only by how many spikes occur.
Why latency suits discrete sampling.
One spike per pulse is enough to report amplitude.
The code operates within each discharge cycle.
Spike counts and spike times.
A neuron can encode a stimulus in how many spikes it fires and in when it fires them.
Here the time of the first spike carried the amplitude.
Link to sampling.
The latency depends on the recent sequence of sensing events, which later slides examine.
Terminology.
A mormyromast is an electroreceptor organ, and its afferent carries information toward the brain.
Latency refers to the first recorded afferent spike.

inserts.title: Adaptation sets the reference for amplitude coding
paragraphs: Adaptation is a change in the responsiveness of a neuron after recent stimulation. A neuron that adapts reports changes relative to the level that it has recently experienced. The carrier is the background level of the signal, and the modulation is the part that an object changes.

Sawtell and colleagues compared afferent responses at different mean local EOD amplitudes, separating the steady carrier level from small amplitude changes superimposed on it. The latency relationship shifted with the mean stimulus.

The same instantaneous amplitude can therefore evoke different latencies under different sensory histories. A decoder in the brain must take the preceding stimulus environment into account when it reads latency as amplitude. The latency therefore reports amplitude relative to a baseline that adaptation adjusts.
notes: The meaning of a spike time depends on the history of the receptor.
Adaptation.
Adaptation is a change in responsiveness associated with recent stimulation.
Carrier and modulation.
The steady carrier level is the mean EOD amplitude at the receptor.
Small amplitude changes are superimposed on it.
Result.
The latency relationship shifted with the mean electric stimulus.
Consequence.
Responses were not determined only by the instantaneous voltage at the receptor.
The preceding stimulus set part of the reference.
Decoding.
The same immediate amplitude can occur under different histories.
Why adaptation exists.
Receptors that adapt keep their responses within a useful range when the mean level changes.
They then report changes around the new level.
Latency relation.
The latency relationship shifted with the mean stimulus, so the same amplitude could give different latencies.
Carrier level.
The carrier level is the steady EOD amplitude at the receptor.
It is distinguished from the smaller modulation that an object introduces.

inserts.title: Brain slices preserve local circuits for recording
paragraphs: A brain slice is a thin section of tissue that is kept alive in solution. The slice preserves the local connections of a region while allowing the experimenter to control stimulation and apply drugs directly. Slice recordings were made intracellularly from identified cells.

Grant and colleagues recorded from cells in slices of the elephantnose ELL, the electrosensory lateral line lobe, a hindbrain structure that receives input from skin electroreceptors. They stimulated deep afferent pathways separately from molecular-layer parallel fibers using 0.1 ms pulses.
Because the organization of the layers is preserved, the two inputs can be compared in the same preparation. Receptor antagonists identify which neurotransmitter receptors mediate each response.
notes: A slice trades the intact animal for control over the circuit.
What a slice is.
A thin section of the brain is kept alive in solution.
Local connections remain intact.
The ELL.
The electrosensory lateral line lobe is a hindbrain structure that receives input from skin electroreceptors.
Two inputs.
Deep afferent pathways and molecular-layer parallel fibers were stimulated separately.
Parallel fibers carry central information across apical dendrites.
Stimulation.
Brief pulses of 0.1 millisecond were used.
Pharmacology.
Receptor antagonists applied to the slice identify which receptors contribute to each response.
Why use pulses of 0.1 milliseconds.
A brief pulse activates fibers at a defined time, so responses can be related to the stimulus.
Interpreting results.
Anatomical identification and pharmacology constrain which pathways and receptors contribute to each recorded response.
Where the recordings were made.
Cells in the elephantnose ELL were recorded intracellularly.
The slice preserved the organization needed to compare the two inputs.

inserts.title: Magnesium and antagonists separate glutamate receptors
paragraphs: AMPA and NMDA receptors are both activated by glutamate, but the NMDA receptor is blocked by extracellular magnesium at negative voltages. Removing magnesium therefore enhances the component of a response that depends on NMDA receptors. A voltage change that favors firing is called an excitatory postsynaptic potential, or EPSP.

Grant and colleagues removed extracellular magnesium and applied CNQX, an antagonist of AMPA receptors, and AP-5, an antagonist of NMDA receptors. Each drug reduced a distinct portion of the evoked response. The experiment measured the effect of each treatment on the evoked response in the same preparation.

Recovery after washout showed that the drug effects were reversible and not caused by tissue failure. The portions removed by the two antagonists identify separate AMPA and NMDA components of excitation.
notes: Two receptor classes can be separated by their voltage dependence and by their antagonists.
Two receptors.
AMPA and NMDA receptors are glutamate-activated ion channels.
Magnesium.
Extracellular magnesium blocks NMDA receptors at negative voltages.
Removing it enhances the NMDA component.
Antagonists.
CNQX blocks AMPA receptors.
AP-5 blocks NMDA receptors.
Result.
Each antagonist reduced a distinct portion of the evoked response.
Reversibility.
Recovery after washout supported a reversible pharmacological effect rather than irreversible tissue failure.
Reading the drugs.
A drug that reduces the response shows that its target receptor contributes to the response.
Two antagonists acting on different receptors can remove different portions.
Controls.
After the drug was washed out, the response recovered.
Recovery shows that the effect is reversible and that the tissue remained healthy.
Excitatory potentials.
An excitatory postsynaptic potential is a synaptically evoked voltage change that favors neuronal firing.
It is the response that the antagonists reduced, and its time course shows how long excitation lasts after the stimulus.

inserts.title: Short-term facilitation depends on pulse spacing
paragraphs: Short-term facilitation is an increase in the response to a second stimulus that follows the first closely. The synapse is temporarily stronger because of its recent activity. The increase is temporary and returns to baseline after a delay.

Grant and colleagues stimulated parallel fibers twice and recorded larger second EPSPs in medium ganglion cells. Facilitation depended on the interval between the pulses and was strong at short intervals, including about 30 ms. The experiment tested several intervals so the time course of facilitation could be mapped.

Stimulation at independent sites distinguished repeated recruitment of one fiber population from activation of another. The strength of a parallel-fiber synapse therefore depends on how recently it was active. This form of plasticity lasts for a short time and differs from long-lasting changes.
notes: A synapse can change its strength within milliseconds of its own activity.
Definition.
Paired-pulse facilitation is an increase in the response to a second closely spaced stimulus.
Experiment.
Parallel fibers were stimulated twice.
Second EPSPs in medium ganglion cells were larger.
Interval dependence.
Intervals ranged across tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
Facilitation was strong at short intervals, including about 30 milliseconds.
Control.
Independent stimulation sites distinguished repeated recruitment of the same fibers from activation of another population.
Meaning.
Synaptic efficacy depends on recent activity.
Facilitation.
A second stimulus evokes a larger response than the first because the synapse was recently active.
The effect fades as the interval lengthens.
Intervals.
The experiment varied intervals from tens to hundreds of milliseconds.
Strong facilitation occurred at short intervals such as 30 milliseconds.
Distinguishing populations.
Using independent stimulation sites shows whether a larger second response comes from repeated activation of the same fibers or from a different population.

inserts.title: A corollary discharge marks the animal's own command
paragraphs: A corollary discharge is an internal copy of a motor command that is sent to sensory areas. In the mormyrid ELL, a signal associated with the electric-organ command accompanies the input from the electroreceptors. The signal accompanies each motor command, whether or not an object is nearby.

Sawtell and colleagues recorded medium ganglion cells in vivo and compared command-evoked activity with sensory responses. The preparation separated the motor command signal from an electric stimulus delivered by the experimenter. The recordings were made in the intact animal under controlled conditions.

The command signal tells the cell when the fish itself discharged. The cell can then interpret incoming electrosensory input relative to the timing of the self-generated pulse. Self-generated context allows the cell to relate sensory input to the sensing action.
notes: The brain keeps a record of the animal's own sensing actions.
Definition.
A corollary discharge is an internal signal associated with a motor command.
In the ELL.
Electric-organ command-related input accompanies peripheral electrosensory input.
Experiment.
Medium ganglion cells were recorded in vivo.
Command-evoked activity, sensory responses and spike types were compared.
Separating signals.
The preparation separated the motor command from a stimulus that the experimenter delivered.
Meaning.
The command timing provides context about the sensing action and not an image of an object.
The ELL circuit.
Medium ganglion cells receive electroreceptor input and command-related input.
They are Purkinje-like interneurons with apical dendrites.
Not an image.
A corollary signal marks timing and does not carry an electric image of an object.
Why context is useful.

A cell that knows when the fish discharged can interpret the arriving electric input relative to the pulse that the fish generated, and the same input means something different at different moments of the command cycle.

inserts.title: Spike-timing-dependent plasticity depends on relative timing
paragraphs: In spike-timing-dependent plasticity, the direction of a lasting synaptic change depends on the relative timing of two events. The same pairing can strengthen a synapse at one delay and weaken it at another.

Sawtell and colleagues repeatedly evoked a B spike at delays between about 8 and 110 ms after the electric-organ command and compared command-evoked responses before and after pairing. Pairing near the peak of the response tended to reduce later excitation, whereas earlier or later pairings could enhance it.

Changes in N-spike output accompanied the altered synaptic response. The timing of the B spike relative to the command therefore determines whether the cell's response to the command is reduced or enhanced.
notes: Plasticity in this circuit depends on when a dendritic event occurs relative to the command.
Definition.
Spike-timing-dependent plasticity is a lasting synaptic change whose direction depends on relative timing.
Pairing.
A B spike was repeatedly evoked at delays from about 8 to 110 milliseconds after the command.
Result.
Pairing near the peak of the command response reduced later excitation.
Earlier or later pairings could enhance it.
Link to output.
N-spike output changed with the altered synaptic response.
Meaning.
Command context, dendritic events, synaptic strength and axonal activity are connected in one adaptive mechanism.
Pairing protocol.
A B spike was evoked repeatedly at a defined delay.
Command-evoked responses were compared before and after pairing.
Direction of change.
Pairing near the peak of the command response reduced later excitation.
Earlier or later pairings enhanced it.
Output of the cell.
N spikes are the principal output of the medium ganglion cell.
Changes in N-spike output tie the altered synaptic response to the output event.
